Welcome to today's lecture on linear algebra, specifically the topic of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Let us consider a square matrix A. A non zero vector V is called an eigenvector of A if multiplying A by V only scales V without changing its direction. The scaling factor is called the eigenvalue, usually denoted by the Greek letter lambda. So the defining equation is A times V equals lambda times V. To find eigenvalues, we rewrite the equation as a minus lambda times I times V equals zero. For a non zero solution V to exist, the determinant of a minus lambda I must be zero. This equation is called the characteristic polynomial. Its roots are the eigenvalues of the matrix. Geometrically, an eigenvector points along a direction that the linear transformation only stretches or flips, never rotates. Eigondecomposition allows us to rewrite a matrix as P times D times P inverse, where D is a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. This is extremely useful for computing matrix powers, solving differential equations and principal component analysis in machine learning. Remember, only square matrices can have eigenvalues and a matrix with distinct eigenvalues is guaranteed to be diagonalizable.
